outcome: A November 2025 preprint by Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams proves an asymptotic version of the conjecture — for every ε>0, every sufficiently large n-vertex tree has gracesize gs(T) ≥ (1-ε)n — which moves the problem's own quantity (gracesize, whose value n-1 for every tree is exactly what the conjecture asserts) very close to the conjectured maximum for large trees, but the conjecture itself (gs(T)=n-1 for every tree) remains open.

disputes.summary: The triage record and a web search both surfaced a claim, apparently originating from the automated pre-print review site pith.science ('Pith Review'), that the paper's proof 'has a few holes in the rainbow-matching engine that need fixing' and that a specific lemma (referred to as Lemma 5.4) is not fully verified as written. I could not load the actual Pith review page content (it returned empty via WebFetch, and I did not use raw curl since that required approval I chose not to invoke for a non-essential fetch). Pith.science describes itself as an AI-driven pre-print review platform (three AI referee passes plus a synthesizer), not a human expert digestion — so even if the gap claim is accurate, it is an AI critique of the paper rather than a human expert's finding, and does not by itself establish an error. I could not find any independent human expert commentary (e.g. a blog post, Tao's blog, or peer review report) confirming or refuting this specific concern. The paper does have a v2 (31 July 2026) with no visible revision comment; it may or may not be a response to this concern.

summary: The graceful tree conjecture (every tree admits a graceful labeling, equivalently gs(T)=n-1 for every n-vertex tree) remains fully open. The only substantive development in the window is the November 2025 arXiv preprint 'On the gracesize of trees' by Shoham Letzter, Alexey Pokrovskiy and Ella Williams (arXiv:2511.11331), which proves an asymptotic approximation: for every ε>0 there is n0 such that every tree on more than n0 vertices has gracesize at least (1-ε)n. This is a bound on the problem's own defining quantity (not a restriction to a special class of trees, and not a different question), so it counts as `progress` rather than `partial` or a resolved case — the full conjecture (exact equality gs(T)=n-1, i.e. every edge-difference distinct) is not settled for any specific large tree by this result, only approached in the limit/asymptotically for all sufficiently large trees. No human expert digestion (Tao's blog, a survey update, or a journal acceptance) of this preprint was found within the time available; a v2 was posted 31 July 2026 with no visible changelog, so I could not confirm whether it addresses the verification concern below. On AI involvement: I read the abstract, arXiv metadata, and as much of the PDF as WebFetch could extract, and found no statement by the authors indicating any AI system produced, checked, or otherwise contributed to any part of the proof; the paper is a fully traditional combinatorics preprint. The only AI angle that surfaced is that a website called 'Pith Review' (pith.science), which advertises itself as running AI referee passes over preprints, appears to have flagged an unverified or gappy step in the paper's 'rainbow-matching engine' / a lemma referred to as Lemma 5.4. I was unable to load the actual Pith page content directly (WebFetch returned it empty), so I rely only on a search-engine summary of it, which I do not consider a source I opened and verified — I flag this explicitly as unconfirmed rather than treating it as established. Even if accurate, this would be an AI system critiquing/reviewing human-produced mathematics, not an AI system producing any of the mathematics in the result, so it would not change `ai_role` from `none` under §6.2's rule that only authorial claims of AI-produced content count.
competing_reading: If the Pith Review's flagged gap in the matching lemma is real and the result does not actually hold as stated, the correct status might arguably be `claimed` rather than `progress` (i.e., an unverified claim rather than settled progress), since 'progress' as I've used it presumes the bound is currently believed sound modulo the usual preprint-not-yet-digested caveat. I judged `progress` still correct because (a) I could not confirm the alleged gap from a source I could actually open and read, (b) the flag itself comes from an AI review tool of unclear reliability rather than a named human expert, and (c) two of the three authors (Pokrovskiy, and via Montgomery–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov) have a strong track record on exactly this family of problems (they proved Ringal's conjecture in a related area), making an uncaught fatal gap less likely though not impossible.
what_would_settle_it: Either: (a) successfully loading the actual Pith Review report or a comparable human referee report for arXiv:2511.11331 and reading its specific objection to Lemma 5.4/the rainbow-matching engine, or (b) finding the v2 (July 2026) changelog/comparison to see if it patches a previously acknowledged gap, or (c) a citation or acceptance of the paper by a journal, or independent expert commentary (e.g. a blog post by Tao, Pokrovskiy, or another extremal-combinatorics researcher) discussing the paper's correctness.
